title: Measuring the spin of a spin-1/2 and getting a result of 7
authors: Joseph McGowan, Nicholas Mantella, Noah Baker, Aephraim M. Steinberg
abstract: The weak value of an operator is the average result of measuring that operator on a quantum system given specified initial and final states. The overlap between these states appears in the denominator of the weak value, and thus if that overlap is small, the weak value can be arbitrarily large. In 1988, Albert, Aharonov, and Vaidman proposed a weak Stern-Gerlach experiment which would be able to measure a so-called anomalous weak value, a measurement result which lies out- side of the eigenvalue spectrum of the operator being measured. Though anomalous weak values have been measured in numerous optical systems, here we present the first such realization of this experiment as originally proposed. By placing a Bose-Einstein condensate of 87Rb in a magnetic gradient and performing an unlikely postselection, we measure an effective magnification of a weak magnetic momentum kick (~ 8 $μ$m/s) by a factor of 14. We also demonstrate that increasing the momentum kick decreases the "weakness" of the measurement and reduces the amplification.
summary: The authors report the first experimental realization of measuring an anomalous weak value using a Bose-Einstein condensate of $^{87}	ext{Rb}$ atoms. By performing a weak Stern-Gerlach measurement and utilizing post-selection, they measured a momentum kick amplified by a factor of 14. This work validates the theoretical framework of weak measurements in an atomic platform, demonstrating its potential for advanced quantum sensing.
main_problem: To experimentally realize and measure an anomalous weak value, specifically measuring a component of a particle's spin, as originally proposed by Aharonov et al.
main_result: The experiment successfully demonstrated weak value amplification in an atomic system, measuring an effective magnification of a weak magnetic momentum kick by a factor of 14, corresponding to a weak value of 7(3) for $\sigma_z$.
method: A weak Stern-Gerlach measurement was performed on a Bose-Einstein condensate using post-selection on the final state to extract the anomalous weak value.
model_or_system: The physical system is a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) of $^{87}	ext{Rb}$ atoms trapped in a magnetic gradient. The measurement relies on coupling the spin and momentum via a weak magnetic field gradient.
key_observables: Pointer shift ($\pi$), weak value ($\langle A angle_w$), and the momentum kick ($\delta_p$).
important_parameters: The measurement is sensitive to the momentum kick parameter ($\delta$) and the initial cloud size ($\sigma$).
main_assumptions: The analysis often assumes the initial state is Gaussian for analytical predictions, although the actual atomic cloud profile may deviate.

paper_structure: The paper develops the theory of weak value amplification, details the experimental setup using BECs, presents the measurement of the pointer shift, and compares the results to the theoretical weak value predictions across varying experimental parameters.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, state-of-the-art realization of a fundamental quantum measurement concept (weak values) using ultracold atoms, pushing the boundaries of quantum metrology and quantum measurement theory in AMO physics.

Above is the bare pointer shift, i.e. ⟨pf⟩|ψ⟩= πf, for the postselected state, and below is πf/δp. Shifts were calculated using TF(z) with σ = 25 µm. The lower plot also shows the weak value ⟨f(δ)| σz |i⟩/ ⟨f(δ)|i⟩.

Figure 1 shows simulations of π for various applied momentum shifts δp, along with the calculated weak value. For this measurement, the pointer shift is given by δp ⟨A⟩w. When δp is large, there is no amplification for any δ; π is bounded by ±δp, and spin rotations merely swap the states. Decreasing δp causes the magnitude of the pointer shift to exceed δp in both directions. The maximum shift, however, is always bounded for small δp;

FIG. 2: Experimental data showing the measured momentum shift (pointer position shift) between the two spin components of the BEC. At each value of δ, each pair of images for a single experimental shot is fitted and the centers subtracted, then this value for all pairs is averaged together. Errorbars represent the standard error on the mean for 60 pairs each. The data are shown with the weak value predictions based on the unamplified kick (in black) and with analytic predictions for a Gaussian initial state of equivalent size (in green).
